title: Tariffs won’t fix Asia-Pacific forced labour – enforcement will
gist: US Section 301 forced-labour tariffs face a Court of International Trade challenge on 30 September 2026, but the author argues the binding constraint on the Asia-Pacific's estimated 15 million forced labourers is enforcement design, not trade leverage: mandatory supply-chain due diligence beyond Tier 1, verification instead of attestation, penalties that scale with state capacity, and a pooled regional risk database.

themes.theme: Tariffs as trade leverage, not remedy

insights.claim: Washington's Section 301 forced labour tariffs will be challenged in the US Court of International Trade on 30 September 2026, and the ruling either way will not resolve whether Asia-Pacific forced labour standards actually work.
insights.so_what: A 30 September court date is a discrete catalyst for importers exposed to Section 301 forced-labour lines; but compliance obligations persist regardless of the outcome, so hedging the legal binary alone misreads the risk.
insights.speaker: Cory Searcy

insights.claim: Forced-labour tariffs have been criticised as instruments of trade leverage rather than genuine labour remediation, and supply-chain due diligence rules would not blunt a government's incentive to use trade leverage anyway.
insights.so_what: Expect tariff actions framed on labour grounds to keep recurring as negotiating tools; do not price them as a durable compliance regime.
insights.quote: None of this would stop the next tariff dispute.
insights.locator: None of this would stop the next tariff dispute
insights.speaker: Cory Searcy

insights.claim: An estimated 15 million people remain in forced labour across the Asia-Pacific despite widespread anti-trafficking laws and the ASEAN Convention Against Trafficking in Persons signed in November 2015, showing legislation on the books has not moved outcomes.
insights.so_what: Legal prohibition is not a screen for supply-chain risk; sourcing diligence must be evidence-based rather than jurisdiction-based.
insights.speaker: Cory Searcy

insights.claim: Concentrated forced-labour exposure sits in identifiable sectors: Thailand's fishing industry, Malaysian rubber glove and palm oil production, and Bangladesh's garment sector.
insights.so_what: These four named sector-country pairs are the most likely first targets of any import ban, procurement blacklist or verification regime — screen suppliers there first.
insights.locator: Examples of forced labour are easy to find
insights.speaker: Cory Searcy

insights.claim: Enforcement capacity across the Asia-Pacific is radically uneven, ranging from democracies with independent regulators to states where enforcement is effectively limited, so any single regional standard will bind unevenly.
insights.so_what: Assume compliance quality varies by jurisdiction regardless of nominal rules; build country-level risk weightings rather than treating a regional convention as coverage.
insights.locator: Any recommendations on how to do so
insights.speaker: Cory Searcy

themes.theme: Disclosure regimes produce paperwork, not change

insights.claim: Australia's Modern Slavery Act, in force since 2019, required supply-chain reporting but attached no financial or criminal penalty for a weak filing, which the author treats as proof that disclosure-only regimes fail.
insights.so_what: Disclosure-based modern slavery statements carry near-zero signal value for screening counterparties; treat them as unaudited marketing until penalties attach.
insights.quote: disclosure without penalty can produce polished reports
insights.locator: Australia's experience also shows the limitations
insights.speaker: Cory Searcy

insights.claim: Australia's Anti-Slavery Commissioner released Recommendations to Strengthen Modern Slavery Laws in January 2026 pushing beyond disclosure to a minimum due diligence obligation — a conclusion reached before the US tariffs were imposed.
insights.so_what: Australian reporting entities should expect a shift from reporting to enforceable due diligence; the timing shows the driver is domestic policy, not US trade pressure, so it survives any court ruling.
insights.speaker: Cory Searcy

insights.claim: The core recommendation is a due diligence obligation extending beyond Tier 1 suppliers to at least second-tier subcontractors, with further tiers added as capacity develops, using the EU Forced Labour Regulation as a reference point.
insights.so_what: Multinationals sourcing in Asia should budget for sub-tier supplier mapping — a materially higher cost base than current Tier 1 attestation programmes.
insights.locator: The starting point is to establish a due diligence obligation
insights.speaker: Cory Searcy

insights.claim: The evidentiary bar should move from attestation to verification, with auditors supported by remote auditing technologies such as satellite-based vessel monitoring to flag fishing vessels operating without required tracking and to target unannounced audits.
insights.so_what: A structural demand driver for satellite/remote-sensing compliance analytics if verification mandates spread; also a new detection channel that can strand non-compliant seafood supply.
insights.locator: Any due diligence obligations should move the evidentiary bar
insights.speaker: Cory Searcy

insights.claim: Penalties should scale with state capacity along an escalating ladder — public disclosure of non-compliance, procurement blacklisting, fines, then criminal penalties — rather than being imposed uniformly.
insights.so_what: Procurement blacklisting is the most commercially damaging middle rung and the most likely to be adopted early; watch government supplier lists as the leading indicator.
insights.speaker: Cory Searcy

themes.theme: Pooled data as the low-friction first move

insights.claim: Sector- and region-specific risk data modelled on the database required under Article 8 of the EU's Forced Labour Regulation is the underpinning requirement, with inputs already produced by the ILO, Human Rights Watch and Goodweave but scattered across NGO reports and foreign customs filings.
insights.so_what: Data aggregation is the cheapest, earliest-moving piece of the regime — an opening for compliance-data vendors well before binding rules land.
insights.locator: Sector- and region-specific risk data is needed
insights.speaker: Cory Searcy

insights.claim: Pooling forced-labour risk data regionally is the most politically realistic starting point because it does not depend on any single country's political system or enforcement capacity.
insights.so_what: If regional cooperation appears anywhere first, expect it in shared risk data rather than binding regulation — a lower bar and an earlier signal to watch.
insights.quote: Pooling this data across the Asia-Pacific is not contingent on any one country’s political system or capacity, making it a realistic starting point for collaboration.
insights.locator: Pooling this data across the Asia-Pacific
insights.speaker: Cory Searcy
